For most of its history the United States addressed civilian harm through policy and discretionary payments, not statute. The Foreign Claims Act covers only noncombat harm. Starting in 2017, Congress wrote a framework into the annual defense authorizations: a public annual casualty report, a required civilian casualty policy with a senior official, a standing ex gratia authority for combat harm, and a Civilian Protection Center of Excellence in Title 10. The Leahy Laws apply the same logic to foreign partners. Since 2025 the main question has been how far the Defense Department may scale these programs back while the statutes remain in force.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain why the Foreign Claims Act does not cover combat harm and what fills the gap.
- List the four civilian harm statutes enacted from FY2018 to FY2023 and what each requires.
- Describe the 2025 and 2026 dispute over statutory compliance.

[Foreign Claims Act](../../statutes/foreign-claims-1942.qmd) [1942]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Targeted provision]{.layer-badge}

Lets the military departments appoint claims commissions to settle claims by inhabitants of foreign countries for property loss, injury, or death caused by U.S. forces or incident to their noncombat activities abroad.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/55/880), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/2734?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="foreign-claims-1942"> I have read this</label>

::: {.reading-card .domain-civilian-protection data-statute="civcas-report-2017"}
[Civilian Casualty Report](../../statutes/civcas-report-2017.qmd) [2017]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Targeted provision]{.layer-badge}

Requires the Secretary of Defense to report to the congressional defense committees by May 1 each year on civilian casualties caused by U.S. military operations in the previous year.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/91), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/113?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="civcas-report-2017"> I have read this</label>

::: {.reading-card .domain-civilian-protection data-statute="civcas-policy-2018"}
[Civilian Casualty Policy](../../statutes/civcas-policy-2018.qmd) [2018]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Targeted provision]{.layer-badge}

Directs the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy to designate a senior civilian official, at or above the Assistant Secretary level, to develop and oversee compliance with Defense Department policy on civilian casualties from U.S. military operations.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/232), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/134?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="civcas-policy-2018"> I have read this</label>

::: {.reading-card .domain-civilian-protection data-statute="ex-gratia-2019"}
[Ex Gratia Payments](../../statutes/ex-gratia-2019.qmd) [2019]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Targeted provision]{.layer-badge}

Authorizes the Secretary of Defense to make ex gratia payments to foreign civilians for property damage, injury, or death incident to the use of force by U.S. forces, a coalition that includes the United States, or a military organization supporting either.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/116/public/92), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/2731?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="ex-gratia-2019"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-civilian-protection data-statute="cp-coe-2022"}
[Civilian Protection Center](../../statutes/cp-coe-2022.qmd) [2022]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Targeted provision]{.layer-badge}

Requires the Secretary of Defense to operate a Civilian Protection Center of Excellence as the Department's focal point for civilian casualties and other civilian harm from U.S. military operations.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/117/public/263), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/184?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="cp-coe-2022"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-aid-sanctions data-statute="leahy-laws"}
[Leahy Laws](../../statutes/leahy-laws.qmd) [1997]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Targeted provision]{.layer-badge}

Two parallel provisions that bar U.S. assistance to any unit of a foreign security force when there is credible information that the unit committed a gross violation of human rights.

[Read it: [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/2378d?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="leahy-laws"> I have read this</label>

::: {.reading-card .domain-war-powers data-statute="dta-2005"}
[Detainee Treatment Act](../../statutes/dta-2005.qmd) [2005]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Targeted provision]{.layer-badge}

Known as the McCain Amendment, it prohibits cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment of anyone in U.S. custody, wherever held, and ties Defense Department interrogations to the Army Field Manual.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/109/public/148), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/42/2000dd?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="dta-2005"> I have read this</label>

## Further reading

- [Military Commissions Act](../../statutes/mil-commissions-2006.qmd){.subj}: Passed after Hamdan v. Rumsfeld struck down the commissions created by presidential order, it gave statutory authority to try alien unlawful enemy combatants by military commission and defined the offenses and procedures.
- [UCMJ](../../statutes/ucmj-1950.qmd){.subj}: The criminal code and court system of the U.S. armed forces. It replaced the separate Army and Navy disciplinary codes with one law for all services, defining military offenses, the types of courts-martial, the rights of the accused, and civilian appellate review.
- [2001 AUMF](../../statutes/aumf-2001.qmd){.subj}: Enacted a week after the September 11 attacks, this joint resolution authorizes the President to use all necessary and appropriate force against the nations, organizations, or persons that planned, authorized, committed, or aided the attacks, or that harbored those who did.
- [Women, Peace & Security Act](../../statutes/wps-2017.qmd){.subj}: Makes it U.S. policy to promote the meaningful participation of women in conflict prevention, peace negotiations, and post-conflict recovery, and requires a government-wide strategy to carry that out.
- [Elie Wiesel Act](../../statutes/wiesel-2018.qmd){.subj}: Declares that preventing genocide and other atrocities is a national interest of the United States and requires the executive branch to organize, train, and report accordingly.
- [Arms Export Control Act](../../statutes/aeca-1976.qmd){.subj}: Governs U.S. arms exports. It sets the purposes for which American weapons may be sold, requires licenses for commercial sales, and gives Congress advance notice of major sales and a procedure to block them.

## Key terms

**Civilian harm mitigation and response**
:   The Defense Department's term, abbreviated CHMR, for preventing, mitigating, and responding to civilian casualties and other harm from military operations.

**Ex gratia payment**
:   A voluntary payment to a harmed civilian or family that does not admit legal liability. Since 2019, Sec. 1213 of the FY2020 NDAA is the sole authority for such payments for harm from the use of force.

**Combat exclusion**
:   The Foreign Claims Act's bar on claims arising from combat, which is why combat harm needs a separate ex gratia authority.

**Center of Excellence**
:   The Civilian Protection Center of Excellence at 10 U.S.C. 184, the Department's statutory focal point for civilian harm data, guidance, and lessons learned.

## Issues for Congress

Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

### 1. Is the Defense Department meeting the civilian harm statutes?

Staffing for civilian harm functions was sharply reduced in 2025 and 2026 while [10 U.S.C. 184](../../statutes/cp-coe-2022.qmd) and the [Civilian Casualty Policy](../../statutes/civcas-policy-2018.qmd) remained in force.

- Those who see noncompliance argue a greatly reduced staff cannot carry out functions Congress wrote into law.
- Others argue the functions can be performed by a smaller staff integrated into existing organizations.

### 2. Should vetting or reporting extend to how partners use U.S. weapons in combat?

The [Leahy Laws](../../statutes/leahy-laws.qmd) address gross violations of human rights by units; proposals in recent Congresses would add reporting on partners' compliance with the law of armed conflict.

- Supporters argue the United States shares responsibility for how its weapons are used and needs information to make transfer decisions.
- Opponents argue added conditions burden partners in active conflicts and duplicate existing end-use monitoring and policy reviews.

## Check yourself

Try to answer each question before opening it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 1. Why can't someone harmed in a U.S. airstrike claim under the Foreign Claims Act?

The act excludes claims arising from enemy action or resulting directly or indirectly from U.S. combat, apart from some aircraft accidents. Combat harm is addressed through [ex gratia payments](../../statutes/ex-gratia-2019.qmd) instead. See [Foreign Claims Act](../../statutes/foreign-claims-1942.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 2. What must the annual civilian casualty report include, and when is it public?

Each operation with confirmed or reasonably suspected civilian casualties, with date, location, authority used, and casualty estimates, plus reasons for discrepancies with outside reporting. The unclassified report is published when submitted unless the Secretary certifies a national security threat. See [Civilian Casualty Report](../../statutes/civcas-report-2017.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 3. What must the senior civilian official designated under Sec. 936 do?

Develop, coordinate, and oversee compliance with civilian casualty policy, including uniform standards for recording strikes, investigating allegations, acknowledging harm, and offering ex gratia payments. See [Civilian Casualty Policy](../../statutes/civcas-policy-2018.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 4. Why could the Defense Department not simply abolish the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence in 2025 and 2026?

Because Congress put it in Title 10 at 10 U.S.C. 184 with specific functions, so ending it requires a change in law. The dispute became whether a sharply reduced staff still satisfies the statute. See [Civilian Protection Center](../../statutes/cp-coe-2022.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 5. How do the Leahy Laws relate to the civilian harm statutes?

The civilian harm statutes govern U.S. operations; the [Leahy Laws](../../statutes/leahy-laws.qmd) condition assistance to foreign units on the absence of credible information of gross human rights violations. Both members' records include bills to extend vetting or reporting to partner operations.
:::
